endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Automated decision-making systems should never create or exacerbate overall or disparate access barriers to needed benefits by increasing denials, coverage limitations, or limiting benefit offerings.

endorsements.title: Prompt engineering for generative artificial intelligence chatbots in health research: A practical guide for traditional, complementary, and integrative medicine researchers
endorsements.quote: Researchers must therefore approach GenAI chatbot-generated content with caution and always verify outputs through manual searching and consultation with librarians or methodological experts.

evidence.title: Evaluation and Comparison of Ophthalmic Scientific Abstracts and References by Current Artificial Intelligence Chatbots
evidence.outcome: Fabricated references in AI-generated scientific text
evidence.effect: High hallucination rate of fake references (33% earlier, 29% updated version); caution advised for academic use.
evidence.quote: There was a high hallucination rate of generating fake references, and caution should be used when using these AI resources for health education or academic purposes.
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot-generated abstracts and references across 7 ophthalmology subspecialties

evidence.title: Learning to Fake It: Limited Responses and Fabricated References Provided by ChatGPT for Medical Questions
evidence.outcome: Fabricated references and factual errors in AI-generated text for medical manuscripts
evidence.effect: 69% of references fabricated; median quality score 60% (Q1 50%, Q3 85%); 5 major and 7 minor factual errors among 17 evaluated responses.
evidence.quote: Users of ChatGPT should pay particular attention to the references provided before integration into medical manuscripts.
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT responses rated by expert authors (20 questions; 59 references evaluated)

evidence.title: Can ChatGPT be trusted as a resource for a scholarly article on treatment planning implant-supported prostheses?
evidence.outcome: Reliability of ChatGPT as a source for synthesizing literature for scholarly articles
evidence.effect: Rated on 4 indices (retrievable source, representative literature, accurate interpretation, conclusion reflects best evidence); concluded ChatGPT could not reliably synthesize the literature for the 6 questions.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT has not demonstrated the ability to accurately cull the literature, stratify the rigor of the evidence, and extract accurate implications from the studies selected to deliver the best evidence-based answers to questions on treatment planning implant-supported prostheses.

evidence.title: Citation Hallucination Determines Success: An Empirical Comparison of Six Medical AI Research Systems
evidence.outcome: Citation hallucination rates in AI-generated research manuscripts across six systems
evidence.effect: Hallucination rates ranged from 2.9% to 36.8% across systems; hard-rule citation threshold capped four of six systems' total scores at the penalty ceiling.
evidence.quote: Hallucination rates ranged from 2.9% to 36.8% across systems, and a hard-rule threshold on per-task citation scores capped four of six systems’ total scores at the penalty ceiling.
evidence.sample_unit: AI research systems (evaluated on 3 NHANES clinical epidemiology tasks)

evidence.title: Citation reliability of frontier large language models in medical writing and its automated verification
evidence.outcome: Proportion of problematic references in LLM-generated medical manuscripts verified against PubMed
evidence.effect: Problematic references were 11.5% of GPT-5.5 output, 29.2% of Claude output, and 29.6% of Gemini output (P < 0.001); misattribution made up 77% of errors, fabrication 0.6%.
evidence.quote: Problematic references accounted for 11.5% of GPT-5.5 output, 29.2% of Claude output, and 29.6% of Gemini output (P < 0.001), with no significant gradient across topics of differing publication volume (P = 0.052).

commentary.bottom_line: No study tests whether journal policies requiring authors to verify AI-generated text and references reduce fabricated or erroneous content in medical literature. Five descriptive and benchmark studies document the hazard, with problematic reference rates ranging from 2.9% to 69% depending on the system and design.

perspectives.view: No study compares manuscripts or journals with and without an author verification requirement, so certainty about the practice cannot be rated. The five hazard studies use descriptive or benchmark designs, and three rest on small samples (6 questions, 17 responses, 6 systems). They measure the size of the problem, not the effect of any remedy.

One study found 69% of 59 references fabricated and 5 major factual errors among 17 responses. A benchmark reported citation hallucination rates of 2.9% to 36.8% across six systems. These figures suggest unverified AI text may carry errors into literature clinicians rely on, though no study traces such errors to patient harm.

A benchmark that checked 8,050 references against PubMed found that misattribution made up 77% of errors and fabrication 0.6%. This suggests a check limited to whether a reference exists may miss most problems. Verification would need to confirm that each source supports its attached claim, and no study has measured the time or fidelity of that step.

One of the two endorsing sources addresses automated coverage denials and does not speak to manuscript verification. The other is a commentary urging manual checking with librarians or methodologists. The recommendation therefore rests on one directly relevant endorsement, and neither source describes how journals would enforce or audit author attestations.

None of the five studies involves patients or reports whether its test questions concerned Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether reference errors occur more often in research on these groups, where the literature base may be thinner, has not been examined.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare reference accuracy and factual error rates in published manuscripts before and after journals adopt AI verification requirements, or between journals with and without such policies. Audits should measure author compliance with attestations, distinguish fabrication from misattribution, and record the reviewer and author time that verification requires.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests the practice, and none of the hazard studies included or reported on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence cannot show whether verification policies would protect the literature that informs care for these groups.
